title: Physical clocks and NTP
summary: Understand local clock drift, the absence of a global clock, and round-trip delay estimation in NTP.
objectives: Separate physical synchronization from causal ordering

sections.title: Physical time is local and imperfect
sections.body: Each process has its own internal physical clock. Clock drift accumulates error, and a distributed system has no automatically available global clock. Synchronization protocols can estimate offset, but they do not turn physical time into causal truth.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The physical/logical distinction is examinable because distributed algorithms need ordering even when synchronized wall-clock time is noisy.

sections.title: NTP as a delay estimate
sections.body: NTP uses four timestamps to estimate round-trip delay and the server time observed by a client. Treat the estimate as a synchronization aid with network-delay assumptions, not as a proof that one distributed event caused another.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The formula is a compact calculation checkpoint and a direct contrast with logical clocks: synchronization estimates time; logical clocks encode causal order.

examples.title: NTP reasoning checklist
steps: Use half the estimated delay for the server-time estimate.
State the network symmetry assumption before interpreting the result.
examples.answer: A numeric timestamp estimate is meaningful only with its delay and synchronization assumptions.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which clock abstraction is designed to preserve causal precedence rather than estimate UTC?
contrastDrills.explanation: Logical clocks are defined by event-order consistency; physical clocks approximate wall-clock time.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the ordering, time, or communication boundary before choosing.

math.explanation: NTP estimates round-trip delay by subtracting the server-side elapsed interval from the client-side elapsed interval.
math.name: NTP round-trip delay estimate
math.purpose: Use it to estimate network delay from the four timestamps in the synchronization exchange.

math.explanation: Under the lecture's delay-symmetry approximation, the client estimates the server time at receipt by adding half the round-trip delay to the server receive timestamp.
math.name: NTP server-time estimate
math.purpose: Use it under the symmetric-delay assumption to estimate remote physical time, not causality.
math.caveat: The estimate depends on network-delay assumptions and does not establish causal precedence.

criticalQuestions.prompt: If $\delta$ is large, what should you question before trusting the synchronized time?
criticalQuestions.angle: Inspect network asymmetry, queueing, and clock drift.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A large delay widens uncertainty; the estimate may be poor even if the arithmetic is correct.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does NTP synchronization not replace logical time?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare a wall-clock estimate with an event-order guarantee.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: NTP estimates physical time. Logical clocks are designed to preserve causal precedence even when physical clocks drift or messages are delayed.
